observation: Datacenter networks must serve cloud applications that require extremely low latency and high bandwidth, yet traffic is commonly bursty and emerging reconfigurable datacenters introduce rapid bandwidth changes, making congestion control a key enabler or limiter of system performance. The reaction time and accuracy of existing datacenter congestion control schemes are inherently limited because they react either only to the absolute network state (queue length, delay, ECN, or loss, called voltage) or only to state variations (e.g., RTT gradient, called current). A voltage-based reaction is oblivious to the rate at which the queue builds up and over-reacts when the queue drains, losing throughput; a current-based reaction is oblivious to the absolute queue length and, having no unique equilibrium, cannot stabilize queue lengths. Consequently, neither class of algorithms alone can deliver both fast, accurate reaction to perturbations and the strict near-zero-queue, high-throughput equilibrium that datacenter workloads demand.

claims: The dominant class of datacenter congestion-control schemes reacts to the instantaneous network state: queue occupancy, ECN marking, packet delay, or packet loss.
DCTCP uses switch-level ECN marking triggered by queue length, and the sender reduces its window in proportion to the fraction of marked packets in a round.
DCQCN carries switch ECN information to RDMA NICs through congestion notification packets and uses queue-threshold-triggered marks as the central congestion feedback.
HPCC replaces threshold marking with per-hop queue lengths and link utilization from in-band network telemetry, letting senders compute an exact current rate.
Such controls have no direct access to the rate of change of the queue signal, so their response is delayed until the absolute signal has already built or drained.

works.title: DCQCN: Congestion Control for Large-Scale RDMA Deployments

claims: A second class of datacenter congestion control targets the variation of delay rather than its absolute level.

TIMELY is a datacenter protocol that computes the RTT gradient in the NIC and adjusts the sending rate in response to this gradient, anticipating queue growth rather than waiting for queue-level thresholds.
A control law based solely on a differentiated congestion signal has no absolute reference to the current queue length and hence no stable target at which the queue must rest.
Therefore current-only control can prevent queue growth but cannot maintain a strict near-zero-queue equilibrium across changing traffic conditions.

works.title: TIMELY: RTT-based Congestion Control for the Datacenter

claims: Datacenter protocols that do obtain near-zero queues generally replace distributed congestion control with scheduling or priority mechanisms.
Homa uses receiver-driven priorities and receiver-side queue information to schedule short flows ahead of bulk traffic, keeping queues short without a conventional sender-rate controller.

Fastpass centralizes transmission decisions in a scheduler that admits packets only when switch buffers will not form queues, providing near-zero-queue transmission at the cost of a centralized arbiter.
These scheduling-based designs are not built around the congestion-control signal classes used by sender-side protocols and require mechanisms outside the standard host transport stack.

works.title: Homa: A Receiver-Driven Low-Latency Transport Protocol Using Network Priorities

claims: Reconfigurable datacenter networks such as RotorNet periodically change which switch pairs are connected, exposing flows to bottleneck capacities that vary independently of host traffic demand.

The queue-threshold and RTT-gradient congestion-control protocols described above were designed for fixed-capacity network paths and do not incorporate knowledge of the timescale at which a reconfigurable link changes.

Consequently, prior sender-side controllers founded on either absolute queue state or its derivative alone cannot simultaneously deliver the fast perturbation tracking and stable near-zero-queue operation that reconfigurable datacenter workloads require.

works.title: RotorNet: A Scalable, Reconfigurable Datacenter Network
TIMELY: RTT-based Congestion Control for the Datacenter

solution.idea: The failure of the two existing classes is a missing state coordinate, not a missing tuning knob. A congestion-controlled bottleneck is naturally a two-state process: the observable queue length is the integral of the mismatch between the offered rate and the current service rate, and the queue’s derivative carries the current mismatch. Voltage-only schemes close the loop on the first coordinate only; because they act through an integrator and have no velocity information, they react after a queue has already formed or already drained, causing overshoot and throughput loss. Current-only schemes close the loop on the second coordinate only; because their feedback signal is zero at every constant queue length, they have no fixed reference and cannot hold the queue at a target. The proposed solution restores both coordinates: the sender runs a proportional-derivative controller on queue occupancy, but uses the resulting command to change the sending rate, not to set the rate directly. The absolute queue length is the proportional term and anchors the equilibrium at a small target queue Q_ref; the queue growth rate is the derivative term and provides damping and early reaction, before the absolute signal crosses any threshold. With this structure an empty queue yields a positive acceleration because Q < Q_ref, so capacity is probed without artificial additive-increase terms; a queue that is still near zero but growing causes damping immediately; and a queue that is above target with a negative derivative, i.e. draining, is not punished as harshly as a voltage-only controller would punish it. The equilibrium is unique: Q = Q_ref and queue growth zero, with the sending rate equal to the current bottleneck service rate. For reconfigurable datacenter paths, the current signal is measured from the schedule-aware instantaneous service rate rather than from RTT gradients, so a change in link capacity is visible in the growth-rate signal at the first control tick instead of after the queue has reacted. This combination avoids the centralized scheduler of Fastpass and the receiver-priority mechanism of Homa, keeping the solution inside the sender-side transport stack while satisfying the datacenter requirements of fast perturbation tracking and near-zero queuing.
solution.implementation:
The implementation has four components: switch-side measurement, telemetry feedback, the sender-side rate controller, and reconfiguration-schedule handling.

(1) Switch-side measurement. Each output queue of every switch keeps two physical counters/signals: Q_h, the current queue occupancy in bytes, and G_h, the current queue growth rate in bytes per second. G_h is computed by the switch as the difference between the aggregate arrival rate into that queue and the current scheduled service rate of the port. The service rate is read from the switch’s reconfiguration schedule when the port is a RotorNet-style reconfigurable port, or from the fixed port speed otherwise. G_h is not a numerically differentiated Q_h; it is the physical derivative of the backlog, and it can be negative when the port is underutilized and the queue is empty. This is important: negative G_h is interpreted as spare capacity by the controller.

(2) Telemetry feedback. Each packet that leaves a switch carries a small HPCC-style in-band telemetry extension containing the pair (Q_h, G_h) for that output queue. The receiver echoes this extension on the ACK path. When no INT-capable switching gear is present, a fallback is to estimate Q from the excess of RTT over the propagation minimum and G from a smoothed RTT gradient, as TIMELY does; the same controller is used, only with noisier signals. On the sender, the telemetry reports are timestamped with the arrival time of the feedback. Reports are consumed on a fixed control period T_c; if several reports arrive inside one period they are aggregated by selecting the most congested hop among them, as described next.

(3) Sender-side rate controller. For each path, the sender keeps a smoothed sending rate R. To convert telemetry into a scalar control sample, first choose the bottleneck hop. For each reported hop compute P_h = Q_h + T_lookahead * max(G_h, 0). T_lookahead is a small prediction horizon, typically a few queue-service times, specifying how far ahead the controller wants to see queue growth. Select the hop with the largest P_h; if all P_h are zero or negative, select the hop with the largest G_h, i.e. the least idle path, because that is where queue will form first. Let Q_n and G_n be the occupancy and growth rate of the selected hop. The continuous control law is

      dR/dt = omega^2 * (Q_ref - Q_n) - 2 * zeta * omega * G_n

where Q_ref is the target occupancy, omega is the natural frequency of the closed-loop second-order response, and zeta is the damping ratio. The discrete update at every control tick is

      dt = T_c
      a_n = omega^2 * (Q_ref - Q_n) - 2 * zeta * omega * G_n
      R_new = R_old + dt * a_n
      R = clamp(R_new, 0, max_host_rate)

The rate R is enforced by a NIC hardware rate limiter or by pacing packet transmissions at microsecond granularity. A small Q_ref, on the order of one Maximum Transmission Unit at the selected bottleneck, is mandatory because Q_ref = 0 would make the controller blind when the queue is empty; with Q_ref > 0, an empty queue appears as a negative error and the rate accelerates until the service capacity is reached. The parameter omega is chosen from the desired settling time T_set, e.g. omega = 1/T_set, and zeta is set at or slightly above 1 to avoid queue oscillation. The control period T_c must be smaller than the RTT and smaller than the closed-loop time constant so that the sampled control loop is stable; a typical choice is a few microseconds. Loss is treated as an emergency signal: upon any packet loss the sender halves R and temporarily reduces Q_ref to absorb the event, although the feedback loop should normally prevent losses.

(4) Reconfiguration-schedule handling. The measurement of G_h already makes the controller schedule-aware because G_h uses the current service rate of the reconfigurable port as the dequeue rate. When the RotorNet schedule changes a port’s service rate at a future time, the switch can compute, before the queue changes, an updated G_h = arrival_rate - new_scheduled_service_rate at the reconfiguration boundary. The first telemetry report generated after that boundary therefore carries the new current signal immediately. The sender does not need to receive a separate schedule feedforward, but it must run at a control period T_c that is no larger than half of the shortest reconfiguration period so that reconfiguration events are not aliased. If a schedule table is available locally, the switch precomputes the sequence of service rates and stamps the next G_h one control period ahead with the predicted arrival rate; this is a purely optional refinement. Because the voltage path, Q_n, is always present, even a completely unpredicted capacity change is eventually absorbed by the proportional term, while the current term prevents the queue from building far past Q_ref in the first place. The resulting system keeps queues near Q_ref, uses feedback from both absolute and differentiated state, and operates under fast, externally scheduled reconfigurations without requiring central per-packet arbitration.
